sections.h2: What is Little Rock, Arkansas, and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Little Rock is the capital and most populous city of Arkansas and the seat of Pulaski County. It sits on the south bank of the Arkansas River near the center of the state, with the Census Bureau estimating 206,427 residents for 2025, up from 202,591 in 2020.

The land is not uniform. Fourche Creek and Rock Creek run through the city to the river, and the western side climbs into the Ouachita Mountain foothills, with Pinnacle Mountain and Lake Maumelle just northwest of the city limits. Lake Maumelle supplies the city's drinking water. North Little Rock lies across the river as a separate city.

Named neighborhoods and districts include Hillcrest, The Heights, Quapaw Quarter, Downtown, South End, West End, Southwest Little Rock, Chenal Valley and Pulaski Heights. A house in the older central neighborhoods and a house in a newer western subdivision face different buyers, different upkeep and different storm exposure.

sections.h2: How did Little Rock get started?
sections.html:
Little Rock was founded on June 1, 1821, as the capital of the Arkansas Territory, became a town in 1831 and was incorporated as a city in 1835. Its name goes back to a riverside rock formation that French explorer Jean-Baptiste Benard de la Harpe named in 1722.

The territorial capital moved from Arkansas Post, which had flooding problems, to this site. The city adopted a council-manager form of government in November 1957, and the mayor has been a full-time position with veto power since 2007. Frank Scott Jr. was elected mayor in November 2018.

sections.h2: Who are the biggest employers in Little Rock?
sections.html:
Healthcare, banking, transportation and retail are the main sectors, and the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences is among the largest employers with more than 10,552 workers. The City of Little Rock itself employs over 2,500 people.

Many of those jobs are in public institutions and hospitals. Colleges also add renters and buyers: the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, UAMS, Philander Smith College, Arkansas Baptist College and Pulaski Technical College are all in or near the city.

sections.h2: What is Little Rock's climate like, and how does it affect a house?
sections.html:
Little Rock has hot, humid summers and cool winters with little snow. The July average daily high is about 91.7 degrees and the January average high is about 50.5 degrees. Annual precipitation averages 50.42 inches and average snowfall is 3.8 inches. The record high is 114 degrees, set on August 3, 2011.

Heat and humidity are hard on roofs, HVAC systems and crawl spaces, and buyers' inspectors check all three. Tornadoes are the sharper risk. The National Weather Service notes that the last EF3-level tornado before 2023 hit Little Rock on January 21, 1999, during a state-record outbreak of 56 tornadoes, and that it killed three people.

On March 31, 2023, an EF3 tornado with 165 mph winds started in the Martindale area and moved northeast through Chenal Valley, Breckenridge, Cammack Village and Burns Park. A city count listed 2,648 structures damaged or destroyed, and 588 properties took major damage. Insurance claims paid in Little Rock exceeded $489 million by the end of 2023, a figure that also includes other severe weather that day.

sections.h2: Which roads, transit and schools serve Little Rock homes?
sections.html:
Little Rock is served by seven interstate routes in the area: I-40, I-30, I-57 (partly unbuilt), I-430, I-440, I-630 and I-530. Clinton National Airport, reached from I-440, has eight passenger airlines and one cargo carrier. Rock Region Metro runs the bus routes, and the Metro Streetcar covers 3.4 miles with 14 stops. Amtrak's Texas Eagle stops twice daily.

The Little Rock School District serves most of the city and has five public high schools: Central, Southwest, West, Hall STEAM Magnet and Parkview Arts and Science Magnet. Where your house sits in relation to a school zone affects who is likely to want it, so know the attendance zone before you talk numbers.

sections.h2: What do Little Rock code enforcement and historic rules mean for sellers?
sections.html:
Little Rock's Code Enforcement Division handles overgrown lots, trash, illegal dumping, non-running vehicles, graffiti, unsecured vacant houses, dilapidated structures and minimum housing code violations. Residents report problems through a Neighborhood Resource Center or by calling 3-1-1. Residential structures that Code Enforcement declares unsafe go to the Board of Directors for condemnation, and then the city contracts for demolition.

  • Code Enforcement Division: 500 West Markham Street, Room 120, phone (501) 379-1516.
  • Central complaint line: 3-1-1.
  • An unsecured or fire-damaged house can be condemned, which makes a sale harder through normal channels.

Historic rules apply in only one local district. The city has 27 National Register historic districts, but listing is honorary and places no restrictions on private owners. Only the MacArthur Park Local Historic District requires a Certificate of Appropriateness before exterior work, site design changes or demolition. Capitol Zoning District rules cover property near the Capitol.

sections.h2: How do Pulaski County recording and property taxes work in a Little Rock sale?
sections.html:
Deeds for Little Rock property are recorded at the Pulaski Circuit and County Clerk's Real Estate Department, Room 102, 401 West Markham Street. The office is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and takes filings in person, by mail or through approved e-recording vendors.

  • Fee: $15 for the first page and $5 for each additional page.
  • Required: original signatures, a grantor and grantee, a Prepared By statement, a Transfer of Tax form and notarization.
  • Photo ID: required since August 5, 2025 under Act 752, except for attorneys, brokers, financial institution representatives and government representatives.
  • Free online recording was scheduled to be unavailable from October 5, 2026 during a land records system change, so use an approved vendor if you file electronically.

The state transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration. Pulaski County's total taxable value was $10,277,025,426 in 2024. Arkansas collects property taxes from the first business day of March through October 15 of the following year, and unpaid taxes after that date carry a 10 percent penalty. Counties reappraise every four years under Act 139 of 2023, homestead taxable value can rise 5 percent a year, and appeals to the county board of equalization must be scheduled by the third Monday in August.

sections.h2: What are your selling options in Little Rock?
sections.html:
You can list through an agent, sell yourself or take a cash offer. Little Rock has a wide range of homes, so a renovated house in Hillcrest and a dated rental in the southwest may take completely different routes.

  • House with code violations: ask the city what is open before you sign anything.
  • Storm damage: an as-is sale avoids a repair bid.
  • Inherited property: confirm who has authority to sign.
  • Rental with tenants: a buyer may take the property subject to the lease.

faqs.q: How many people live in Little Rock, Arkansas?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimates 206,427 residents as of 2025, after the 2020 census counted 202,591.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit or certificate to sell a house in Little Rock?
faqs.a: The city's historic preservation page describes the certificate only for exterior work, site changes and demolition. Only owners in the MacArthur Park Local Historic District need a Certificate of Appropriateness, before that kind of work.

faqs.q: Where is a deed recorded for a Little Rock house?
faqs.a: At the Pulaski Circuit and County Clerk's Real Estate Department, 401 West Markham Street, Room 102, Little Rock. The fee is $15 for the first page and $5 for each extra page.

faqs.q: What happens if my Little Rock house is condemned?
faqs.a: After Code Enforcement declares a residential structure unsafe, it goes to the city's Board of Directors for condemnation, and the city can contract for demolition. Contact Code Enforcement at (501) 379-1516 to learn what applies to your property.

faqs.q: Was Little Rock hit by the 2023 tornado?
faqs.a: Yes. The March 31, 2023 EF3 tornado crossed west Little Rock, including Chenal Valley and Breckenridge, and a city count listed 2,648 structures damaged or destroyed.

faqs.q: When are Pulaski County property taxes due?
faqs.a: By October 15 of the year after assessment. A 10 percent penalty applies to unpaid taxes after that date.
